recipe.history:
Cauliflower — Brassica oleracea var. botrytis — belongs to the enormous family of cultivated brassicas that also includes broccoli, kale, Brussels sprouts, and cabbage, all descended from a wild mustard plant native to the Mediterranean coast. Cauliflower's precise origins are debated, but it was likely first developed in the Arab-controlled Mediterranean world — possibly Cyprus or the Arab agricultural revolution in Spain — and Arab agricultural writers were describing varieties of heading brassicas in the twelfth century. It arrived in France and England in the sixteenth century, carried by Arab traders and then French merchants, where it was immediately embraced by courtly kitchens as a refined, expensive vegetable that required skill to cook properly. For much of the following four centuries, cauliflower was treated primarily as a delicate boiled or gratin vegetable — pale, finely textured, and mild, best accompanied by cheese sauce or cream. The vegetable's blandness was its virtue in classical European cooking: it provided body and substance without competing with the other flavors on the plate. What changed everything for cauliflower in American cooking was the discovery that high-heat roasting — particularly in a very hot oven or under a broiler — transformed it from a mild, watery vegetable into something with a deeply caramelized, nutty, almost meaty exterior while the interior softened into something almost creamy. This revelation arrived in American restaurant cooking in the early 2000s and by the 2010s had spawned the 'cauliflower steak' trend: a thick cross-section of a cauliflower head, roasted or griddled with olive oil and spices until the flat faces develop a golden-brown crust, served as a vegetarian main or, in this case, as an extraordinary burger topping.

Cauliflower's arrival as a serious topping in American burger culture is part of the broader movement toward vegetable-forward cooking that reshaped American restaurant menus in the 2010s. Chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi popularized the idea that vegetables could be treated with the same intensity and technique applied to meat — charred, spiced, brined, and roasted to develop deeply complex flavors. The cauliflower steak became a symbol of this movement: a vegetable cut and cooked like a piece of meat, capable of developing the same Maillard-reaction browning, the same textural contrasts, the same satisfying depth. On a burger, a thick slab of roasted cauliflower adds both structural interest and a flavor that is simultaneously sweet, nutty, earthy, and slightly bitter — qualities that interact with the savory richness of ground beef in ways that raw or simply steamed cauliflower never could. The BETTER CAULIFLOWER SAUL BURGER — a pun on the television series Better Call Saul — pairs this roasted cauliflower steak with a harissa-spiced mayo and tahini drizzle, bringing the cauliflower's Middle Eastern culinary heritage full circle.

I became a convert to roasted cauliflower on a burger after a long period of skepticism. I had eaten enough badly prepared cauliflower — the boiled-into-mush variety that turns gray at the edges and smells vaguely of damp basement — to have reservations. Then one evening I cut a one-inch slab from the center of a large head, seasoned it aggressively with olive oil, smoked paprika, cumin, garlic powder, and salt, and put it in a 450-degree oven on a preheated cast iron pan. The sound when it hit the pan was the sound of transformation: a hiss of steam and fat that meant caramelization was already beginning. Twenty minutes later it came out looking like a piece of seared tuna — deeply golden on both sides, slightly charred at the edges, fragrant with spice. I put it on a medium-rare beef patty and ate the whole thing in approximately four minutes. I owe cauliflower an apology for all the years I underestimated it.

The medium-rare beef patty is the essential foundation of this burger, and its importance is amplified by the nature of the cauliflower topping. The roasted cauliflower steak is substantial — it has real body, real flavor, and real textural presence. The only patty that can hold its own beneath it is one cooked to 130–135 degrees Fahrenheit, still juicy and pink, still assertive in flavor, still possessing the quality of having been treated with respect. A well-done patty would collapse texturally and flavor-wise under the weight of a cauliflower steak and a harissa mayo — you would essentially be eating a spiced cauliflower sandwich on bread. The medium-rare patty keeps the beef at the center of the conversation where it belongs.
ingredients: 2–4 tbsp water (to thin to drizzling consistency)
fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes. Rise in oiled bowl 1 hour. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash; sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes. Cool on rack.

2. Prepare the cauliflower steaks: Preheat oven to 450°F (232°C). Place a large cast-iron skillet or heavy baking sheet in the oven while it preheats. Remove the outer leaves of the cauliflower but leave the core intact. Cut from the center 4 steaks approximately 3/4 to 1 inch thick. (Reserve the florets that fall off for another use.) Whisk together olive oil, smoked paprika, cumin, garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, salt, and pepper in a small bowl. Brush both sides of each cauliflower steak generously with this spiced oil.

3. Carefully remove the preheated skillet from the oven. Working quickly, lay the cauliflower steaks flat on the hot surface. Return to the oven. Roast 15 minutes, then carefully flip each steak. Roast another 10–12 minutes until both sides are deeply golden-brown and the centers are tender when pierced with a knife. Remove and keep warm.
4. Make the harissa mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, harissa paste, lemon juice, and honey. Season with salt. Refrigerate.

5. Make the tahini drizzle: Whisk together tahini, lemon juice, and grated garlic. Add water one tablespoon at a time until the sauce reaches a pourable, drizzling consistency. Season with a pinch of salt.

6. Form the patties: Combine ground beef with cumin, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season outside with additional salt just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Lay a slice of provolone on each patty. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes off heat.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread harissa mayo on both bun halves. Place a leaf of romaine lettuce and a tomato slice on the bottom bun. Place the provolone-topped patty on top. Lay a roasted cauliflower steak over the patty. Add red onion slices. Drizzle tahini sauce over the cauliflower. Scatter a few fresh parsley leaves on top. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
